title: Web framework: jobs, health checks and secrets
description: Scheduled and background jobs, multi-instance duplicate runs, Actuator and FastAPI health checks with liveness vs readiness, plus configuration and secrets handling.
source: Spring Framework scheduling docs; Spring Boot Actuator docs; ShedLock README; FastAPI BackgroundTasks docs; Celery docs; Kubernetes probe docs; redis-py docs
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.

questions.prompt: @Scheduled(cron = "0 0/15 * * * *") uses Spring's six-field cron (second minute hour day month weekday). How many times per hour does the method fire?
questions.explanation: Seconds=0, minutes=0/15 means minutes 0, 15, 30, 45 of every hour: 4 runs. Spring cron has a leading seconds field, unlike Unix cron.

questions.prompt: A Spring app with a nightly @Scheduled cleanup job is deployed as 3 identical replicas and nothing coordinates them. How many times does the cleanup run each night across the cluster?
questions.explanation: Each instance has its own scheduler, so the job runs 3 times. Fixes: a distributed lock (ShedLock, Redis SET NX, DB advisory lock), a leader election, or a dedicated scheduler instance or Kubernetes CronJob.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A @Async method called from another method of the same class runs synchronously on the caller's thread.
questions.reason: The async behaviour is applied by a proxy, and an internal this.call() bypasses that proxy.

whys.a: Correct: no proxy, no executor hand-off.

questions.explanation: Put async methods on another bean, and remember @EnableAsync. Same pitfall as @Transactional and @Cacheable.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: FastAPI BackgroundTasks run after the response has been sent.
questions.reason: BackgroundTasks run in the same process as the web server, so they are lost if that process dies.

whys.a: Wrong: where they run does not explain when they run.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but R is a separate durability limitation, not the reason for the timing.

questions.explanation: Good for small jobs like e-mails. For retries, durability or heavy CPU work use Celery, RQ, Arq or a queue.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Celery tasks should be written to be idempotent.
questions.reason: Celery guarantees exactly-once execution by default.

whys.c: Correct: A is true, R is false; delivery is at-least-once, especially with acks_late or visibility timeouts.

questions.explanation: Redelivery after a worker crash or timeout can run a task twice, so use idempotency keys or upserts.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Spring's @Scheduled tasks run on a pool of 10 threads by default.
questions.reason: A @Scheduled method must take no arguments.

whys.d: Correct: the default scheduler is single-threaded (Boot's spring.task.scheduling.pool.size defaults to 1); R is true because the method must be void-compatible and argument-free.

questions.explanation: One slow job can delay all others. Set spring.task.scheduling.pool.size or use your own TaskScheduler.

questions.prompt: Write a FastAPI POST /signup handler signup(email: str, tasks: BackgroundTasks) that queues send_welcome_email(email) to run after the response and answers with status code 202.
questions.explanation: The task function and args are passed separately to add_task. Both async and plain functions are accepted.

questions.prompt: Python with redis-py: at the start of a scheduled job, take a lock so only one instance runs it. Use the single atomic call that sets key lock:nightly only if it does not exist, expiring after 300 seconds, and return early if the lock was not acquired.

checks.label: sets a TTL with ex= (or px=)
returns when the lock was not acquired

questions.explanation: SET NX EX is atomic, unlike SETNX followed by EXPIRE. Pick a TTL longer than the job, or renew it. Java equivalents: ShedLock's @SchedulerLock, or Redisson locks.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring Boot Actuator health indicator bean PaymentsHealth for a boolean method gateway.ping(): report UP when true, otherwise DOWN with the detail "gateway" set to "unreachable".
questions.explanation: A bean named PaymentsHealth appears as payments in /actuator/health. Beware: adding a flaky dependency to the aggregate health can mark the whole app DOWN.

questions.prompt: Write GET /health/ready for FastAPI. Call db_ping() (raises on failure); on success return {"status": "ok"}, on failure answer HTTP 503.
questions.explanation: A JSONResponse(status_code=503) is equally fine. Keep readiness cheap and time-boxed.

questions.prompt: Match each probe or endpoint with what it means in Kubernetes / Spring Boot.

right.text: The pod is removed from Service endpoints but is not restarted
Other probes wait until a slow boot has finished

questions.explanation: Boot exposes /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness probe groups (enabled automatically on Kubernetes, or via management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled).

questions.prompt: Your service depends on a database. Where should the DB check live to avoid a restart storm during a DB outage?

options.text: In readiness only; liveness should reflect only that the process itself is healthy.
options.why: Readiness failure stops traffic without killing pods.

options.text: In the liveness probe, so that pods that cannot reach the database are restarted quickly.
options.why: A DB outage would restart every pod and extend recovery.

options.text: In both probes with the same timeout.
options.why: This still triggers restarts of healthy processes.

options.text: In neither; health checks must never touch dependencies.
options.why: Readiness checks on critical dependencies are standard.

questions.explanation: Spring Boot's readiness group excludes external systems by default and liveness is for unrecoverable internal states.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are sound practices for configuration and secrets?

options.text: Inject passwords via environment variables or a secrets manager.
options.why: Keeps secrets out of the repository and image.

options.text: Use @ConfigurationProperties with @Validated to fail fast on missing config.
options.why: Binding validation stops the app at startup rather than at first use.

options.text: Use SecretStr in pydantic settings so values are masked in repr and logs.
options.why: get_secret_value() is required to read it.

options.text: Commit application-prod.yml with the production DB password.
options.why: Anything in git history is compromised.

options.text: Log all settings at startup to help debugging.
options.why: That writes secrets into log aggregation.

options.text: Bake the API key into the Docker image.
options.why: Anyone who can pull the image can read it.

questions.explanation: Principle: config in the environment (12-factor), secrets from a vault, validate at boot, never log them.

questions.text: Bind a property prefix to a typed class with {1}; Spring maps the environment variable {2} onto spring.datasource.url; pydantic hides a value in repr and logs by typing it as {3}.
questions.explanation: @Value is for single properties. Relaxed binding upper-cases and replaces dots with underscores, so SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL works.

questions.prompt: Write a Spring Boot immutable configuration class MailProps for properties under prefix app.mail with a String host and an int port, as a record bound by @ConfigurationProperties.

checks.label: is a record (or class) named MailProps
has String host and int port

questions.model:
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.mail")
public record MailProps(String host, int port) {}
questions.explanation: Register with @EnableConfigurationProperties(MailProps.class) or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan. Add @Validated and constraints for fail-fast startup.
